environment.md
globals.md
http.md
other_protocols.md
# HTTP collection files

Read when authoring HTTP request, example, or definition YAML. These field
shapes distinguish v3 files from exported collection JSON; validate edits with
collection lint before relying on the result.

## Definition file (`.resources/definition.yaml`)

Optional metadata for a collection or folder:

- `$kind: "collection"` — required, even for a folder's definition.
- `name` — optional, defaults to the filesystem folder name.
- `description` — optional.
- `variables` — array of `{key, value, description?, disabled?}`. `value`
  must be a string; `disabled` a boolean. A map of name to value is also
  accepted when no entry needs `description` or `disabled`.
- `auth` — a single auth object `{type, credentials: [{key, value}, ...]}`
  or an array for multiAuth: `[{id, name, type, credentials, rules?}, ...]`.
  `credentials` may also be a map of key to value.
- `scripts` — array of `{type, code, language: "text/javascript"}`. `type`
  is one of `http:beforeRequest`, `http:afterResponse`,
  `graphql:beforeQuery`, `graphql:afterResponse`, `grpc:beforeInvoke`,
  `grpc:onIncomingMessage`, `grpc:afterResponse`.
- `order` — number, used for folder ordering.

## HTTP request (`*.request.yaml`)

- `$kind: "http-request"` — required.
- `name` — optional (see naming rules below for when to include it).
- `order` — number; only used for relative comparison, so space values out
  (e.g. multiples of 1000) rather than packing them tight — a later
  insertion between two requests shouldn't force renumbering every sibling.
- `url` — string, with `{{varName}}` variable syntax.
- `method` — `GET|POST|PUT|DELETE|PATCH|HEAD|OPTIONS`.
- `headers` — array of `{key, value, description?, disabled?}`, or a map of
  header name to value when no entry needs `description` or `disabled`.
- `queryParams` — array of `{key, value, description?, disabled?}`.
- `pathVariables` — array of `{key, value, description?}`.
- `body` — `{type, content}`; `type` required whenever `body` is present.
  - Types: `json`, `formdata`, `urlencoded`, `text`, `xml`, `html`,
    `javascript`, `file`, `none`.
  - `json`/`text`/`xml`/`html`/`javascript`: `content` is a string.
  - `formdata`: `content` is an array of
    `{key, type: "text"|"file", value or src, contentType?, description?}`.
  - `urlencoded`: `content` is an array of `{key, value, description?}`, or a
    map of key to value.
- `auth` — `{type, credentials}`.
- `settings` —
  `{protocolVersion?, strictSSL?, followRedirects?, maxRedirects?, disabledSystemHeaders?}`.
- `scripts` — array of `{type: "beforeRequest"|"afterResponse", code, language: "text/javascript"}`.
- `examples` — optional, a relative path to the examples directory, e.g.
  `./.resources/<request-name>.resources/examples/`.

When editing query parameters, update both places they are recorded: the
query string in `url` and the entries in `queryParams`. Their names, values and
order must match; lint reports a difference as `FMT209`: a different value or
order, an entry in only one of the two, or `queryParams: []` next to a query
string. Disabled `queryParams` entries are ignored by the check, and a query
string in `url` with no `queryParams` key at all is not reported, but write both
so they stay in step. For example, `q=shoes&page=2` is represented as:

```yaml
url: '{{base_url}}/search?q=shoes&page=2'
queryParams:
  - key: q
    value: shoes
  - key: page
    value: '2'
```

## HTTP example (`*.example.yaml`)

`http-example` requires `$kind` and `response`, and `response` requires `body`:

```yaml
$kind: http-example
name: 200 OK
request:
  method: POST
  url: https://api.example.com/orders
  headers:
    - key: Content-Type
      value: application/json
  body:
    type: json
    content: '{"sku":"A1"}'
response:
  statusCode: 200
  statusText: OK
  headers:
    - key: Content-Type
      value: application/json
  body:
    type: json
    content: '{"id":"o_1"}'
order: 1000
```

For a saved `204 No Content` example, the YAML schema still requires a
`response.body` object. Represent the absence of response content with
`body: {type: text, content: ''}`. This describes the saved example file;
it does not add content to the HTTP response.

Response `body.type` accepts only `text`, `json`, `xml`, `html`, `javascript`
and `yaml`. For a form-encoded response, use `type: text` with a
matching `Content-Type` header. Request bodies do have `urlencoded`.

Saved examples feed **ai-readiness**, documentation, and mocks; a structurally
valid example still needs to agree with the contract.

## Environments (`postman/environments/*.environment.yaml`)

Environment files are v3 YAML but are not collection entities: they do not use
`$kind`. Before creating or editing one by hand, read
[reference/environment.md](environment.md) for the schema, secret
handling, CLI-first edit commands, and a linted example.

## Auth

`auth` is available on a collection, a folder, a request and an example. It has two
shapes. No auth:

```yaml
auth:
  type: noauth
```

Anything else takes `type` plus `credentials`:

```yaml
auth:
  type: bearer
  credentials:
    - key: token
      value: '{{TOKEN}}'
```

`type` is one of `basic`, `bearer`, `apikey`, `digest`, `oauth1`, `oauth2`, `jwt`,
`awsv4`, `hawk`, `ntlm`, `asap`, `edgegrid`, `azure`, `sasl`, `inherit`. Use `inherit`
to take the parent folder's or collection's auth explicitly; omitting `auth` entirely
does the same thing.

`credentials` keys are the same names the Postman app shows for that auth type —
`username`/`password` for `basic`, `token` for `bearer`, `key`/`value`/`in` for
`apikey`, `accessKey`/`secretKey`/`region`/`service` for `awsv4`. A structurally
valid credential entry does not establish that the server will authenticate it.
`credentials` is an array of `{key, value}` entries.

## Request body

`body` is one shape chosen by `type` — write that branch's keys and nothing else.

```yaml
body: {type: none}
```
```yaml
body:
  type: json          # or text, xml, html, javascript
  content: |-
    {"id": 1}
```
```yaml
body:
  type: urlencoded
  content:
    - key: grant_type
      value: client_credentials
```
```yaml
body:
  type: formdata
  content:
    - key: file
      type: file
      src: ./payload.bin
    - key: note
      type: text
      value: hello
      contentType: text/plain
```
```yaml
body:
  type: file
  content:
    src: ./upload.bin       # an object with src, not a bare path
```

Choose `body.type` to match the payload and contract. JSON `content` is a string;
a block scalar keeps it readable without turning it into a YAML object.
A *response* body inside an example has a narrower type list:
see [HTTP examples](#http-example-exampleyaml).

## Scripts

```yaml
scripts:
  - type: afterResponse
    code: |-
      pm.test('ok', () => pm.response.to.have.status(200));
```

`type` is `beforeRequest` or `afterResponse` on a request, and protocol-prefixed on a
collection or folder (`http:beforeRequest`, `http:afterResponse`,
`graphql:beforeQuery`, `grpc:beforeInvoke`, …). The request-level types for
GraphQL and gRPC are listed with those request kinds in `other_protocols.md`;
lint does not check a script's `type`. A script entry may also carry
`language`, `packages`, and `requests`. `language` takes exactly one value,
**`text/javascript`** — `language: javascript` is a hard error,
`Invalid input: expected "text/javascript"`. Omitting it is fine.

The v2.1 `event:` field is not the v3 `scripts:` field. A script's `type` also
depends on its scope; moving it between a request and a definition requires checking
the type as well as the code. See the main skill's verification guidance for
checking that the intended script behavior survives the edit.

## YAML rules

YAML parsing and scalar coercion can change a field's meaning before schema
validation. Preserve the type the field expects:

1. Single-quote any value containing `{{variables}}`:
   `url: '{{base_url}}/users'` — never leave it unquoted.
2. Single-quote values containing `: # & * ! [ ] { } > |`, e.g.
   `name: 'Health check: v2'`.
3. Multi-line content (JSON bodies, scripts, queries) uses a `|-` block
   scalar:
   ```yaml
   body:
     type: json
     content: |-
       {
         "name": "example"
       }
   ```
4. Quote strings that resemble booleans/numbers when a string is intended:
   `value: "true"`, `value: "123"`.
5. `order` must be a bare number, never quoted: `order: 1000`.
6. Single-quote file paths and use forward slashes only:
   `examples: './.resources/name.resources/examples'`.

## Naming rules

- `<request-name>` (the filename stem before `.request.yaml`) must not
  contain `/ \ : * ? " < > |` — sanitize to `-`.
- Include `name` in the file only when it differs from `<request-name>`
  (e.g. `name: 'Health/check'` inside `Health-check.request.yaml`, since the
  filename itself can't hold the `/`).
- Filenames must be unique, case-insensitively, per directory.

## Worked example: "bookstore api"

`postman/collections/bookstore api/get all books.request.yaml`
```yaml
$kind: http-request
method: GET
url: '{{base_url}}/books'
order: 1000
```

`postman/collections/bookstore api/get-book-by-id.request.yaml`
```yaml
$kind: http-request
name: 'get book by :id'
method: GET
url: '{{base_url}}/books/:id'
order: 2000
pathVariables:
  - key: id
    value: '1'
```

`postman/collections/bookstore api/add new book.request.yaml`
```yaml
$kind: http-request
method: POST
url: '{{base_url}}/books'
order: 3000
headers:
  - key: Content-Type
    value: application/json
body:
  type: json
  content: |-
    {
      "title": "Example Book",
      "author": "Jane Doe"
    }
```

`postman/collections/bookstore api/.resources/definition.yaml`
```yaml
$kind: collection
name: Bookstore API

output:

```bash

  --environment "postman/environments/Staging EU.environment.yaml"

  --environment "postman/environments/Staging EU.environment.yaml"

  - `key` — required variable name.

    values containing YAML punctuation or `{{variables}}` so YAML does not
    coerce them.
  - `enabled` — boolean. The CLI writes `true` for a newly set variable.

    for sensitive values.

    also a recognised way to mark a secret.
  - `description` — optional string.

`variables`. Do not put secrets into an example merely to make it executable;
leave the value empty or use the team's supported secret source.

values:
  - key: baseUrl
    value: 'https://staging.example.com'
    enabled: true
    type: default
    description: API base URL
  - key: apiToken
    value: ''
    enabled: false
    type: secret

`postman workspace lint` when the task is to validate the entire local

# HTTP collection files

Read when authoring HTTP request, example, or definition YAML. These field
shapes distinguish v3 files from exported collection JSON; validate edits with
collection lint before relying on the result.

## Definition file (`.resources/definition.yaml`)

Optional metadata for a collection or folder:

- `$kind: "collection"` — required, even for a folder's definition.
- `name` — optional, defaults to the filesystem folder name.
- `description` — optional.
- `variables` — array of `{key, value, description?, disabled?}`. `value`
  must be a string; `disabled` a boolean. A map of name to value is also
  accepted when no entry needs `description` or `disabled`.
- `auth` — a single auth object `{type, credentials: [{key, value}, ...]}`
  or an array for multiAuth: `[{id, name, type, credentials, rules?}, ...]`.
  `credentials` may also be a map of key to value.
- `scripts` — array of `{type, code, language: "text/javascript"}`. `type`
  is one of `http:beforeRequest`, `http:afterResponse`,
  `graphql:beforeQuery`, `graphql:afterResponse`, `grpc:beforeInvoke`,
  `grpc:onIncomingMessage`, `grpc:afterResponse`.
- `order` — number, used for folder ordering.

## HTTP request (`*.request.yaml`)

- `$kind: "http-request"` — required.
- `name` — optional (see naming rules below for when to include it).
- `order` — number; only used for relative comparison, so space values out
  (e.g. multiples of 1000) rather than packing them tight — a later
  insertion between two requests shouldn't force renumbering every sibling.
- `url` — string, with `{{varName}}` variable syntax.
- `method` — `GET|POST|PUT|DELETE|PATCH|HEAD|OPTIONS`.
- `headers` — array of `{key, value, description?, disabled?}`, or a map of
  header name to value when no entry needs `description` or `disabled`.
- `queryParams` — array of `{key, value, description?, disabled?}`.
- `pathVariables` — array of `{key, value, description?}`.
- `body` — `{type, content}`; `type` required whenever `body` is present.
  - Types: `json`, `formdata`, `urlencoded`, `text`, `xml`, `html`,
    `javascript`, `file`, `none`.
  - `json`/`text`/`xml`/`html`/`javascript`: `content` is a string.
  - `formdata`: `content` is an array of
    `{key, type: "text"|"file", value or src, contentType?, description?}`.
  - `urlencoded`: `content` is an array of `{key, value, description?}`, or a
    map of key to value.
- `auth` — `{type, credentials}`.
- `settings` —
  `{protocolVersion?, strictSSL?, followRedirects?, maxRedirects?, disabledSystemHeaders?}`.
- `scripts` — array of `{type: "beforeRequest"|"afterResponse", code, language: "text/javascript"}`.
- `examples` — optional, a relative path to the examples directory, e.g.
  `./.resources/<request-name>.resources/examples/`.

When editing query parameters, update both places they are recorded: the
query string in `url` and the entries in `queryParams`. Their names, values and
order must match; lint reports a difference as `FMT209`: a different value or
order, an entry in only one of the two, or `queryParams: []` next to a query
string. Disabled `queryParams` entries are ignored by the check, and a query
string in `url` with no `queryParams` key at all is not reported, but write both
so they stay in step. For example, `q=shoes&page=2` is represented as:

```yaml
url: '{{base_url}}/search?q=shoes&page=2'
queryParams:
  - key: q
    value: shoes
  - key: page
    value: '2'
```

## HTTP example (`*.example.yaml`)

`http-example` requires `$kind` and `response`, and `response` requires `body`:

```yaml
$kind: http-example
name: 200 OK
request:
  method: POST
  url: https://api.example.com/orders
  headers:
    - key: Content-Type
      value: application/json
  body:
    type: json
    content: '{"sku":"A1"}'
response:
  statusCode: 200
  statusText: OK
  headers:
    - key: Content-Type
      value: application/json
  body:
    type: json
    content: '{"id":"o_1"}'
order: 1000
```

For a saved `204 No Content` example, the YAML schema still requires a
`response.body` object. Represent the absence of response content with
`body: {type: text, content: ''}`. This describes the saved example file;
it does not add content to the HTTP response.

Response `body.type` accepts only `text`, `json`, `xml`, `html`, `javascript`
and `yaml`. For a form-encoded response, use `type: text` with a
matching `Content-Type` header. Request bodies do have `urlencoded`.

Saved examples feed **ai-readiness**, documentation, and mocks; a structurally
valid example still needs to agree with the contract.

## Environments (`postman/environments/*.environment.yaml`)

Environment files are v3 YAML but are not collection entities: they do not use
`$kind`. Before creating or editing one by hand, read
[reference/environment.md](environment.md) for the schema, secret
handling, CLI-first edit commands, and a linted example.

## Auth

`auth` is available on a collection, a folder, a request and an example. It has two
shapes. No auth:

```yaml
auth:
  type: noauth
```

Anything else takes `type` plus `credentials`:

```yaml
auth:
  type: bearer
  credentials:
    - key: token
      value: '{{TOKEN}}'
```

`type` is one of `basic`, `bearer`, `apikey`, `digest`, `oauth1`, `oauth2`, `jwt`,
`awsv4`, `hawk`, `ntlm`, `asap`, `edgegrid`, `azure`, `sasl`, `inherit`. Use `inherit`
to take the parent folder's or collection's auth explicitly; omitting `auth` entirely
does the same thing.

`credentials` keys are the same names the Postman app shows for that auth type —
`username`/`password` for `basic`, `token` for `bearer`, `key`/`value`/`in` for
`apikey`, `accessKey`/`secretKey`/`region`/`service` for `awsv4`. A structurally
valid credential entry does not establish that the server will authenticate it.
`credentials` is an array of `{key, value}` entries.

## Request body

`body` is one shape chosen by `type` — write that branch's keys and nothing else.

```yaml
body: {type: none}
```
```yaml
body:
  type: json          # or text, xml, html, javascript
  content: |-
    {"id": 1}
```
```yaml
body:
  type: urlencoded
  content:
    - key: grant_type
      value: client_credentials
```
```yaml
body:
  type: formdata
  content:
    - key: file
      type: file
      src: ./payload.bin
    - key: note
      type: text
      value: hello
      contentType: text/plain
```
```yaml
body:
  type: file
  content:
    src: ./upload.bin       # an object with src, not a bare path
```

Choose `body.type` to match the payload and contract. JSON `content` is a string;
a block scalar keeps it readable without turning it into a YAML object.
A *response* body inside an example has a narrower type list:
see [HTTP examples](#http-example-exampleyaml).

## Scripts

```yaml
scripts:
  - type: afterResponse
    code: |-
      pm.test('ok', () => pm.response.to.have.status(200));
```

`type` is `beforeRequest` or `afterResponse` on a request, and protocol-prefixed on a
collection or folder (`http:beforeRequest`, `http:afterResponse`,
`graphql:beforeQuery`, `grpc:beforeInvoke`, …). The request-level types for
GraphQL and gRPC are listed with those request kinds in `other_protocols.md`;
lint does not check a script's `type`. A script entry may also carry
`language`, `packages`, and `requests`. `language` takes exactly one value,
**`text/javascript`** — `language: javascript` is a hard error,
`Invalid input: expected "text/javascript"`. Omitting it is fine.

The v2.1 `event:` field is not the v3 `scripts:` field. A script's `type` also
depends on its scope; moving it between a request and a definition requires checking
the type as well as the code. See the main skill's verification guidance for
checking that the intended script behavior survives the edit.

## YAML rules

YAML parsing and scalar coercion can change a field's meaning before schema
validation. Preserve the type the field expects:

1. Single-quote any value containing `{{variables}}`:
   `url: '{{base_url}}/users'` — never leave it unquoted.
2. Single-quote values containing `: # & * ! [ ] { } > |`, e.g.
   `name: 'Health check: v2'`.
3. Multi-line content (JSON bodies, scripts, queries) uses a `|-` block
   scalar:
   ```yaml
   body:
     type: json
     content: |-
       {
         "name": "example"
       }
   ```
4. Quote strings that resemble booleans/numbers when a string is intended:
   `value: "true"`, `value: "123"`.
5. `order` must be a bare number, never quoted: `order: 1000`.
6. Single-quote file paths and use forward slashes only:
   `examples: './.resources/name.resources/examples'`.

## Naming rules

- `<request-name>` (the filename stem before `.request.yaml`) must not
  contain `/ \ : * ? " < > |` — sanitize to `-`.
- Include `name` in the file only when it differs from `<request-name>`
  (e.g. `name: 'Health/check'` inside `Health-check.request.yaml`, since the
  filename itself can't hold the `/`).
- Filenames must be unique, case-insensitively, per directory.

## Worked example: "bookstore api"

`postman/collections/bookstore api/get all books.request.yaml`
```yaml
$kind: http-request
method: GET
url: '{{base_url}}/books'
order: 1000
```

`postman/collections/bookstore api/get-book-by-id.request.yaml`
```yaml
$kind: http-request
name: 'get book by :id'
method: GET
url: '{{base_url}}/books/:id'
order: 2000
pathVariables:
  - key: id
    value: '1'
```

`postman/collections/bookstore api/add new book.request.yaml`
```yaml
$kind: http-request
method: POST
url: '{{base_url}}/books'
order: 3000
headers:
  - key: Content-Type
    value: application/json
body:
  type: json
  content: |-
    {
      "title": "Example Book",
      "author": "Jane Doe"
    }
```

`postman/collections/bookstore api/.resources/definition.yaml`
```yaml
$kind: collection
name: Bookstore API
variables:
  - key: base_url
    value: 'https://api.bookstore.com/v1'
```

name: api-simulation
description: Use when you add or change code that calls other services and need to run it, test it, prove a fix or reproduce an upstream failure (timeouts, 5xx, 409, 429) end to end, locally or in CI, without the real services because they're unreachable, need credentials, cost money, have side effects or don't exist yet. Also use it to answer what happens to a request, or to the data it writes, when a service it calls goes down, is slow or returns errors ("what happens to a booking if the email service is down?"). Runs services, frontends, tests or demos against stand-ins for their HTTP dependencies, served as one environment locally or at a deployed URL. Applies even when nobody says mock or simulation; a `postman/simulations/` directory is itself a reason to load it. To give a frontend or another team a stand-in for an API, use api-mocking. Covers `postman simulation`.
---

# API Simulation

Simulation lets you control how dependencies behave and explore how your code
responds to different outcomes. This makes it easier to test assumptions
repeatedly without real calls changing data, spending money, or notifying
someone. Simulation context records those assumptions, the evidence supporting
them, and what remains unknown. As sessions build on this context, it helps
surface incorrect assumptions and avoid repeated investigation.

Together, the simulation and its context provide a place to explore changes
and identify what still needs validation against the real dependencies.

Check whether an existing simulation in `postman/simulations/` covers the
dependency interactions relevant to the task. Reusing its mocks and wiring
can avoid rebuilding an environment; extend it only where the behavior you
need to exercise is missing.

The `<name>.context.yaml` beside a simulation records those assumptions, their
supporting evidence, and unresolved questions so later sessions can build on
earlier findings. For example, a timeout from `/payments` does not establish
whether the payment failed or completed before the response arrived. The
context file will document what has been established about the real provider
and identify what still needs verification.

A simulation serves several mocks as one environment: by default behind a
proxy that answers for the dependencies' own hostnames, so the code under test
keeps the base URLs it ships with, or on one local port where each member is
reached by its routeKey.

Simulation adds value when the result depends on real HTTP behavior, such as
client configuration, serialization, timeouts or retries, and the real
dependencies are unavailable or unsuitable for the exercise. Stubbing the
HTTP client can bypass those behaviors. Choose verification that exercises
what matters to the task: an existing test may already answer a local logic
question, while a claim about the provider may need its contract or a real
service check. A simulation's log shows what each stand-in was asked.

Define the expected outcome and what observation would distinguish correct
from incorrect behavior, including side effects when relevant. A request
through the changed path shows that it ran; its response and resulting state
determine whether the expectation held. Choose boundary and failure cases
from the behavior changed and the consequences of getting it wrong.

`postman simulation` needs CLI 1.70.0 or later (`postman --version`; an older
CLI answers `postman simulation -h` with its general help).

## Building it

- **Members are the code's HTTP dependencies.** Databases, queues and caches
  aren't; run them locally. **api-discovery** can find calls made through
  shared code; ask about the repo by its `git remote` name, because a close
  name matches another repo.
- **Each member needs a mock: see `api-mocking`,** which looks for the owning
  team's published mock before building one. Finding and pulling an owner's
  mock needs a signed-in CLI; check `postman status` first, and signed out,
  build each mock and record that the owner search was skipped. For a question, one built from
  the contract will do; one that invents responses can send the caller down a
  path the real service never would. In a mock you build, answer `501` for calls this path
  doesn't make: a `404` reads to the caller like a real "not found".
- **Bring in each mock you don't own as a dependency first, then build the
  simulation over them.** `postman dependency add mock <name-or-id>` declares
  it in `.postman/resources.yaml` and materialises it under
  `postman/.dependencies/`, and the member's `path:` points there; `-w
  <workspace>` resolves a name from the workspace that owns it.
- **Prefix each mock's `pm.state` keys with its name.** As of CLI 1.73.0,
  members of a local run read each other's keys, so two mocks storing
  `orders` overwrite each other.

## Running it

The run is a server that never exits, so a foreground command never returns.
Start it in the background, its log in a file:

```bash
postman simulation run postman/simulations/checkout-dev.sim.yaml --proxy --output ndjson > sim.ndjson 2> sim.err &
```

`--proxy` is how to run it unless something below rules it out: nothing about
the code changes for the run — not a base URL, not a config file, not an SDK's
built-in host — and because nothing the proxy answers for has to resolve, an
internal hostname with no DNS record works.

It's up when `sim.ndjson` has a `listening` event; a start-up error is in
`sim.err`, a busy proxy port among them. Stop it with
`pkill -INT -f "simulation run .*<file>.sim.yaml"`. Nothing reloads: restart
it after a mock edit.

Read `postman simulation run --help` before driving it. The flags, what the
caller's own process needs in order to reach the proxy, and what to do about a
client that ignores it are all there and change with the CLI, so take them
from the command rather than from here.

What decides whether a proxied run proves anything is `origin:`. A member with
none in the `.sim.yaml` is never matched, so its traffic reaches the real
service and a run can come up having intercepted nothing — `simulation create`
copies that field from the mock's manifest, so editing the manifest alone
won't fix it ([reference/sim_yaml_schema.md](reference/sim_yaml_schema.md)).

## Running it on one port instead

`--port` puts every member on one local port, each addressable by its routeKey,
with the code under test pointed at that port. Reach for it when a client has
no proxy setting to honour, and when you want to address a member yourself —
each one keeps a stable URL for the whole run, so a mock's control routes and
its individual responses are a curl away.

## Reading the log

A passing test command doesn't show the dependency path ran: read
`sim.ndjson`. A member with no `request` events isn't wired or isn't on this
path. Some answers come from the simulation itself and mean wiring, not code:

- `404 Unknown simulation member`, on a one-port run: a base URL lost its
  routeKey, or a client sent the wrong `x-mock-slug`.
- `501`, or a generated mock's `404 Endpoint not defined`: a call the mock
  doesn't model yet.
- `502 Proxy error`: the member's process died, usually an async throw in a
  mock without `interceptRequests: true`. It stays down and logs nothing
  until you restart; run that mock alone with `postman mock run` to see why.

## When a dependency goes down

Choose failures from the outcome the user needs to understand. A failure
before a write, a timeout after a write may have completed, and a failure
during compensation can expose different risks: lost work, duplicate writes
or unreleased resources. Read the caller to identify relevant paths, then
exercise the ones whose runtime behavior remains uncertain.

Isolating one failure helps attribute the result. Combine failures or model
partial completion when the question depends on their interaction. The
injection must represent the event being investigated: delaying a response
alone does not establish whether a write completed before the timeout.
Examples of available techniques:

- **Unreachable:** point its base URL at a port nothing listens on. This one
  needs the one-port run, since under `--proxy` the base URLs are the point.
- **Hanging:** give its member a `latency` condition longer than the
  client's timeout. If the client sets none, that is the finding: Node's
  `fetch` waits about five minutes, so say so rather than wait it out.
- **An error with a JSON body:** the `error` condition.
- **An error with an HTML body,** as proxies send: a copy of its mock whose
  default handler answers `500` with HTML. No condition can do this.

Only `overrides.conditions` on a member change it. Members always serve
their default handler and ignore `x-mock-scenario`, and a `scenarios` entry
with just a `path`, as the Postman app writes, does nothing. Fields and the
other conditions are in [reference/sim_yaml_schema.md](reference/sim_yaml_schema.md). An injected
failure never reaches the mock and isn't logged, so judge it by what the
caller did, and check the other members' logs for side effects, such as
stock reserved and never released.

## Its context document

Every simulation is created with a `<name>.context.yaml` beside it, holding
what the code is believed to rely on about the dependencies it calls — who the
caller is taken to be, which plan or permission is assumed, the order calls go
in, what gets retried, the shape of the data — and what each belief rests on.
The `.sim.yaml` says what the simulation is, not what the services it stands in
for do, so this is the record that saves a session the search.

Read relevant claims before investigating the dependencies, and assess whether
their evidence still applies to this task. Write what you established back
into the document before you finish. Each claim carries a `status`,
the `reason` the evidence adds up to it, the `verification` that was done and
what it showed, and a `source` to re-check it against, so the next session can
tell a claim a contract promises from one a request actually demonstrated.
Preserve existing claims and their evidence when updating the file, including
unresolved assumptions and historical findings. Its fixed schema and guidance
on evidence and reuse are in
[reference/context_file.md](reference/context_file.md); read that before
writing to it.

## Keeping it

Commit your own mocks, the `.sim.yaml`, its context document and what
`postman dependency add` changed, so the next session or CI reruns it in one
command. Don't commit
`postman/.dependencies/`: a copy goes stale when its owner updates theirs,
and `postman dependency install` restores it. Don't commit `sim.ndjson`: the
CLI redacts common auth headers and fields, but other headers and bodies are
logged as sent. In CI, `postman dependency install` needs `POSTMAN_API_KEY`,
and `postman collection run <collection> --simulation <file> --port <n>`
starts and stops the simulation around a collection run.

`postman simulation push` uploads every member to the workspace, so ask
first. It fails on a pulled member, which keeps its owner's `id:`; copy it to
`postman/mocks/` and delete that line.

## Rules

1. **What you're testing is never a member.** It must run for real, or the
   test only proves the mock.
2. **Pull the owner's mock even if it's deployed.** Only members take
   conditions and appear in the log, and a private mock server wants a key
   your code won't send.
3. **`simulation deploy` is public by default,** unlike `mock deploy`. Ask
   before deploying without `--private`; a local run needs no deploy.

## Before you say it works

Claim a simulation passes only after the code under test ran and you observed
the expected response or state change. Use its calls in the log to confirm
the dependency path was exercised; for injected failures, use the caller
outcomes described above. If startup failed or the relevant path never ran,
report that limitation. Say what a pass proves,
your code against these stand-ins rather than the real services, what still
needs the real service before release, and where each mock came from,
including when you skipped the owner's.

Then write what you established back into `<name>.context.yaml`, so the next
session starts where this one ended. Add or update claims that help a later
session reuse the findings. For each claim the run settled or contradicted,
update its `status`, the `verification` that was done and the `source` to

name: api-simulation
description: Use when you add or change code that calls other services and need to run it, test it, prove a fix or reproduce an upstream failure (timeouts, 5xx, 409, 429) end to end, locally or in CI, without the real services because they're unreachable, need credentials, cost money, have side effects or don't exist yet. Also use it to answer what happens to a request, or to the data it writes, when a service it calls goes down, is slow or returns errors ("what happens to a booking if the email service is down?"). Runs services, frontends, tests or demos against stand-ins for their HTTP dependencies, served as one environment locally or at a deployed URL. Applies even when nobody says mock or simulation; a `postman/simulations/` directory is itself a reason to load it. To give a frontend or another team a stand-in for an API, use api-mocking. Covers `postman simulation`.
---

# API Simulation

Simulation lets you control how dependencies behave and explore how your code
responds to different outcomes. This makes it easier to test assumptions
repeatedly without real calls changing data, spending money, or notifying
someone. Simulation context records those assumptions, the evidence supporting
them, and what remains unknown. As sessions build on this context, it helps
surface incorrect assumptions and avoid repeated investigation.

Together, the simulation and its context provide a place to explore changes
and identify what still needs validation against the real dependencies.

Check whether an existing simulation in `postman/simulations/` covers the
dependency interactions relevant to the task. Reusing its mocks and wiring
can avoid rebuilding an environment; extend it only where the behavior you
need to exercise is missing.

The `<name>.context.yaml` beside a simulation records those assumptions, their
supporting evidence, and unresolved questions so later sessions can build on
earlier findings. For example, a timeout from `/payments` does not establish
whether the payment failed or completed before the response arrived. The
context file will document what has been established about the real provider
and identify what still needs verification.

A simulation serves several mocks as one environment: by default behind a
proxy that answers for the dependencies' own hostnames, so the code under test
keeps the base URLs it ships with, or on one local port where each member is
reached by its routeKey.

Simulation adds value when the result depends on real HTTP behavior, such as
client configuration, serialization, timeouts or retries, and the real
dependencies are unavailable or unsuitable for the exercise. Stubbing the
HTTP client can bypass those behaviors. Choose verification that exercises
what matters to the task: an existing test may already answer a local logic
question, while a claim about the provider may need its contract or a real
service check. A simulation's log shows what each stand-in was asked.

Define the expected outcome and what observation would distinguish correct
from incorrect behavior, including side effects when relevant. A request
through the changed path shows that it ran; its response and resulting state
determine whether the expectation held. Choose boundary and failure cases
from the behavior changed and the consequences of getting it wrong.

`postman simulation` needs CLI 1.70.0 or later (`postman --version`; an older
CLI answers `postman simulation -h` with its general help).

## Building it

- **Members are the code's HTTP dependencies.** Databases, queues and caches
  aren't; run them locally. **api-discovery** can find calls made through
  shared code; ask about the repo by its `git remote` name, because a close
  name matches another repo.
- **Each member needs a mock: see `api-mocking`,** which looks for the owning
  team's published mock before building one. Finding and pulling an owner's
  mock needs a signed-in CLI; check `postman status` first, and signed out,
  build each mock and record that the owner search was skipped. For a question, one built from
  the contract will do; one that invents responses can send the caller down a
  path the real service never would. In a mock you build, answer `501` for calls this path
  doesn't make: a `404` reads to the caller like a real "not found".
- **Bring in each mock you don't own as a dependency first, then build the
  simulation over them.** `postman dependency add mock <name-or-id>` declares
  it in `.postman/resources.yaml` and materialises it under
  `postman/.dependencies/`, and the member's `path:` points there; `-w
  <workspace>` resolves a name from the workspace that owns it.
- **Prefix each mock's `pm.state` keys with its name.** As of CLI 1.73.0,
  members of a local run read each other's keys, so two mocks storing
  `orders` overwrite each other.

## Running it

The run is a server that never exits, so a foreground command never returns.
Start it in the background, its log in a file:

```bash
postman simulation run postman/simulations/checkout-dev.sim.yaml --proxy --output ndjson > sim.ndjson 2> sim.err &
```

`--proxy` is how to run it unless something below rules it out: nothing about
the code changes for the run — not a base URL, not a config file, not an SDK's
built-in host — and because nothing the proxy answers for has to resolve, an
internal hostname with no DNS record works.

It's up when `sim.ndjson` has a `listening` event; a start-up error is in
`sim.err`, a busy proxy port among them. Stop it with
`pkill -INT -f "simulation run .*<file>.sim.yaml"`. Nothing reloads: restart
it after a mock edit.

Read `postman simulation run --help` before driving it. The flags, what the
caller's own process needs in order to reach the proxy, and what to do about a
client that ignores it are all there and change with the CLI, so take them
from the command rather than from here.

What decides whether a proxied run proves anything is `origin:`. A member with
none in the `.sim.yaml` is never matched, so its traffic reaches the real
service and a run can come up having intercepted nothing — `simulation create`
copies that field from the mock's manifest, so editing the manifest alone
won't fix it ([reference/sim_yaml_schema.md](reference/sim_yaml_schema.md)).

## Running it on one port instead

`--port` puts every member on one local port, each addressable by its routeKey,
with the code under test pointed at that port. Reach for it when a client has
no proxy setting to honour, and when you want to address a member yourself —
each one keeps a stable URL for the whole run, so a mock's control routes and
its individual responses are a curl away.

## Reading the log

A passing test command doesn't show the dependency path ran: read
`sim.ndjson`. A member with no `request` events isn't wired or isn't on this
path. Some answers come from the simulation itself and mean wiring, not code:

- `404 Unknown simulation member`, on a one-port run: a base URL lost its
  routeKey, or a client sent the wrong `x-mock-slug`.
- `501`, or a generated mock's `404 Endpoint not defined`: a call the mock
  doesn't model yet.
- `502 Proxy error`: the member's process died, usually an async throw in a
  mock without `interceptRequests: true`. It stays down and logs nothing
  until you restart; run that mock alone with `postman mock run` to see why.

## When a dependency goes down

Choose failures from the outcome the user needs to understand. A failure
before a write, a timeout after a write may have completed, and a failure
during compensation can expose different risks: lost work, duplicate writes
or unreleased resources. Read the caller to identify relevant paths, then
exercise the ones whose runtime behavior remains uncertain.

Isolating one failure helps attribute the result. Combine failures or model
partial completion when the question depends on their interaction. The
injection must represent the event being investigated: delaying a response
alone does not establish whether a write completed before the timeout.
Examples of available techniques:

- **Unreachable:** point its base URL at a port nothing listens on. This one
  needs the one-port run, since under `--proxy` the base URLs are the point.
- **Hanging:** give its member a `latency` condition longer than the
  client's timeout. If the client sets none, that is the finding: Node's
  `fetch` waits about five minutes, so say so rather than wait it out.
- **An error with a JSON body:** the `error` condition.
- **An error with an HTML body,** as proxies send: a copy of its mock whose
  default handler answers `500` with HTML. No condition can do this.

Only `overrides.conditions` on a member change it. Members always serve
their default handler and ignore `x-mock-scenario`, and a `scenarios` entry
with just a `path`, as the Postman app writes, does nothing. Fields and the
other conditions are in [reference/sim_yaml_schema.md](reference/sim_yaml_schema.md). An injected
failure never reaches the mock and isn't logged, so judge it by what the
caller did, and check the other members' logs for side effects, such as
stock reserved and never released.

## Its context document

Every simulation is created with a `<name>.context.yaml` beside it, holding
what the code is believed to rely on about the dependencies it calls — who the
caller is taken to be, which plan or permission is assumed, the order calls go
in, what gets retried, the shape of the data — and what each belief rests on.
The `.sim.yaml` says what the simulation is, not what the services it stands in
for do, so this is the record that saves a session the search.

Read relevant claims before investigating the dependencies, and assess whether
their evidence still applies to this task. Write what you established back
into the document before you finish. Each claim carries a `status`,
the `reason` the evidence adds up to it, the `verification` that was done and
what it showed, and a `source` to re-check it against, so the next session can
tell a claim a contract promises from one a request actually demonstrated.
Preserve existing claims and their evidence when updating the file, including
unresolved assumptions and historical findings. Its fixed schema and guidance
on evidence and reuse are in
[reference/context_file.md](reference/context_file.md); read that before
writing to it.

## Keeping it

Commit your own mocks, the `.sim.yaml`, its context document and what
`postman dependency add` changed, so the next session or CI reruns it in one
command. Don't commit
`postman/.dependencies/`: a copy goes stale when its owner updates theirs,
and `postman dependency install` restores it. Don't commit `sim.ndjson`: the
CLI redacts common auth headers and fields, but other headers and bodies are
logged as sent. In CI, `postman dependency install` needs `POSTMAN_API_KEY`,
and `postman collection run <collection> --simulation <file> --port <n>`
starts and stops the simulation around a collection run.

`postman simulation push` uploads every member to the workspace, so ask
first. It fails on a pulled member, which keeps its owner's `id:`; copy it to
`postman/mocks/` and delete that line.

## Rules

1. **What you're testing is never a member.** It must run for real, or the
   test only proves the mock.
2. **Pull the owner's mock even if it's deployed.** Only members take
   conditions and appear in the log, and a private mock server wants a key
   your code won't send.
3. **`simulation deploy` is public by default,** unlike `mock deploy`. Ask
   before deploying without `--private`; a local run needs no deploy.

## Before you say it works

Claim a simulation passes only after the code under test ran and you observed
the expected response or state change. Use its calls in the log to confirm
the dependency path was exercised; for injected failures, use the caller
outcomes described above. If startup failed or the relevant path never ran,
report that limitation. Say what a pass proves,
your code against these stand-ins rather than the real services, what still
needs the real service before release, and where each mock came from,
including when you skipped the owner's.

Then write what you established back into `<name>.context.yaml`, so the next
session starts where this one ended. Add or update claims that help a later
session reuse the findings. For each claim the run settled or contradicted,
update its `status`, the `verification` that was done and the `source` to
re-check it against. Scope what you claim to what you actually
exercised — "held in the scenarios run" rather than "works" — since the record
is read later as evidence, and the two don't mean the same thing.
[reference/context_file.md](reference/context_file.md) has what each field is
for.

content.content:
# `.sim.yaml` reference

Read this when writing or debugging a `.sim.yaml` by hand.
`postman simulation create` writes the same shape; the Postman app adds
`id:` fields, which a local run ignores.

```yaml
simulation: checkout-dev               # required: the name
routing: path                          # path (default) or header
mocks:                                 # required: one entry per member
  - name: catalog                      # optional display name
    routeKey: catalog                  # lowercase letters, digits, - and _
    origin:                            # optional: hostnames, for --proxy
      - catalog.internal.example.com
    path: postman/mocks/catalog        # a mock's folder, config.yaml or handler
    scenarios:                         # optional: conditions, below
      - overrides:
          conditions:
            latency: { delay_ms: 250 }
```

Run the `.sim.yaml` rather than a simulation id: a run by id drops every
member's conditions (CLI 1.70.0–1.73.0), and `--proxy` takes no id at all,
since the file is what declares the hostnames.

`simulation create` writes each `path:` relative to the repository root, the
directory holding `postman/`, and puts the simulation in a folder of its own
(`postman/simulations/checkout-dev/checkout-dev.sim.yaml`) so its
`<name>.context.yaml` sits beside it; the app records that document in a
`context:` ref. Reading is broader than writing — a path relative to
`postman/simulations/`, to the file, absolute or `~/`, naming the folder or
the manifest inside it, all resolve — and an unresolvable one names every
directory it looked in.

## Conditions

| Condition | Field | Effect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `latency` | `delay_ms` | Holds each request that long, then serves it. |
| `error` | `status_code` (400–599) | Every request gets that status as JSON, with `"scenario":"error"`. |
| `rate_limit` | `requests_per_minute` | Requests over the limit get `429` and `Retry-After`. |
| `chaos` | `failure_rate` (0–100), optional `status_code` | That share of requests, at random, get `500` or that status. |

- A condition covers every route on its member. To fail one endpoint while
  its siblings succeed, give that endpoint a mock of its own.
- They run in a fixed order (`latency`, `error`, `rate_limit`, `chaos`), and
  the first to fail a request ends it, so set one failure at a time,
  optionally with `latency`.
- An unknown condition name is ignored silently, so a misspelling injects
  nothing. `overrides.bypass` prints a warning and is ignored.
- A `latency` request is served and logged, with a `duration` that leaves
  out the delay.

## `origin`

The hostnames a member answers for under `--proxy`, and the only thing that
decides which member a proxied request reaches.

`simulation create` copies `origin` from the mock's manifest
(`origin: api.stripe.com`, a string or a list).

A scheme and port are stripped (`https://API.Stripe.com:443` →
`api.stripe.com`). An unmatchable value — a path left on a copied URL, a
wildcard — is warned about and skipped, leaving the member working; two
members claiming one hostname fails the run. A member whose mock declares
none has no `origin` key, since `origin: []` would reach the actual service instead of the mock.

Under `--proxy` the members run on throwaway ports, so a manifest's `port` is
ignored.

## The log (`--output ndjson`)

One JSON event per line on stdout; notices go to stderr, so keep them apart.

- `listening`: every member has started; a member that fails to start
  stops the run with `Error: …` and exit code 1.
- `request`: one per request a member served.
- `summary`, on stop: `requestsServed` (under 400), `requestsFailed` (400
  and up), `uptimeMs` and `signal`. Injected failures and the simulation's
  own `400`, `404` and `502` aren't counted.
---
name: api-testing
description: Use when testing an endpoint with real HTTP requests, running collection assertions, or checking real application traffic against an API contract. Not for unit tests of internal functions. Reuses saved requests and reports what live, mocked, or captured-traffic results actually establish. Use for requests such as "test this endpoint".
---

# API Testing

Saved requests preserve the auth, payloads, variables, and assertions that make
an API check reproducible. The useful result is evidence about an intended
guarantee; a successful HTTP exchange alone does not establish correctness.

1. Choose the smallest execution mode that answers the question:

   | Evidence needed | Use |
   | --- | --- |
   | One endpoint with no saved request | `postman request <url>` |
   | Behavior of an existing saved request | `postman collection run <collection-path> -i <request-id-name-or-path>` |
   | Reusable regression checks | `postman collection run <path-or-id>` |
   | Whether a real app's calls match the contract | `postman application test` |
   | An MCP server's tools, resources, or prompts | `postman mcp` (see **mcp-testing**) |

2. Reuse a matching request under `postman/collections/` before reconstructing
   its HTTP fields. Running it through the collection retains inherited auth,
   variables, and scripts. `postman request` takes a URL, not a request YAML
   path; for an unsaved request with an existing payload file, `--body @path`
   preserves that file as the source. See **collection-schema-v3** when
   editing the saved request.
3. Derive assertions from the contract and the behavior at risk. A test that
   merely repeats the current implementation can bless its bug. Preserve
   existing guarantees and add checks for the changed behavior; put reusable
   `pm.test` assertions in the collection so later runs and teammates inherit
   them. Inline `--script-post-request` assertions suit a one-off check.
4. Choose a real or mocked target according to the claim. `--use-mock` lets a
   collection run exercise request and assertion logic without a live
   backend; `--mock` alone only starts one. `--use-mock` replaces the
   variable's whole value, base path included (see **api-mocking**). Passing
   against that mock does not verify the service the mock stands in for.
5. Reuse environment resolution with `-e` and **variables**. Use a CSV/JSON
   file through `-d` for simple iteration; use **datasets** when the inputs
   need queries, joins, or reusable views. Export a report when
   **ci-integration** needs evidence beyond terminal output; it says which
   report formats a collection supports.
6. Use `application test` when the application's actual traffic is the subject.
   It runs an existing command, such as `--command "npx playwright test"`,
   captures its traffic, and matches it against collections. `--capture-only`
   instead exports a v3 collection organized by host; that captures behavior
   without validating it. Results are recorded in the connected workspace by
   default; `--report-events=false` keeps the run local when required.

Use command-specific `-h` for supported options. Workspace resources need a
signed-in CLI; a bare URL or local collection does not require a workspace
binding.

## Verification

Report the target, tested behavior, assertion counts, and exit code. The exit
code reflects failed assertions, not HTTP status alone: a 200 can fail a test.
For application testing, distinguish matching from capture-only mode, and for
mocked runs state which real behavior remains unverified.
---
name: performance-testing
description: Use when load-testing or benchmarking an API with concurrent virtual users and latency or error thresholds, or when importing or migrating a JMeter `.jmx` plan or a Gatling simulation (Java/Kotlin/Scala/JS/TS) into a Postman collection plus a `postman performance run` configuration. Reuses a collection to probe a chosen failure mode and distinguishes target limits from load-generator limits. Use for requests such as "load test this API", "import my JMeter plan", or "convert my Gatling project to Postman".
---

# Performance Testing

A collection supplies realistic request sequences; `postman performance run`
adds concurrency and a load profile. This makes performance claims repeatable,
but only for the workload, data, and network path actually exercised.
Collections run directly: converting with `postman-to-k6` is not required.

1. Choose the failure mode before the profile: `fixed` tests sustained
   concurrency, `ramp-up` explores degradation as load grows, `spike` tests
   sudden surges, and `peak` tests staying near maximum load. Reuse the
   collection's auth and assertions, and check that its operations and data
   represent the workload rather than repeating one unusually cheap request.
2. Establish the target, VU count, duration, and effects of write requests
   before sending load. Existing user authorization for that scope is enough;
   resolve missing limits before stressing a shared or production service.
   Thresholds are evaluated after the run, so a failing gate will not stop
   traffic early. A small initial run can expose wiring failures before a
   larger authorized test.
3. Choose the runner by reachability and capacity. `local` uses this machine
   or CI runner; its CPU or network can become the bottleneck. `postman-cloud`
   moves generation to Postman's infrastructure, while
   `postman-cloud-static-ip` supports targets with IP allowlists. Verify
   reachability before interpreting connection failures as service capacity.
4. Set thresholds that represent the user's objective, such as
   `--pass-if "less_than(p95, 500)"`. Supported metrics include `avg`, `p90`,
   `p95`, `p99`, `error_rate`, and `rps`; latency alone can look good when
   requests fail quickly. Use `postman performance run -h` for current syntax,
   units, and runner-specific options.
5. Isolate test data where concurrent writes would collide. **datasets**
   supports controlled row distribution across VUs; setup/teardown collections
   on hosted runners execute once around the test, not once per iteration.
   `--use-mock` can baseline collection/script overhead, but its numbers
   cannot establish the real backend's capacity.

## Importing from JMeter

Have a JMeter `.jmx` instead of a collection? Import it by following
`references/jmeter-import/README.md`, then treat the result as the collection
above. Its mapping table carries the JMeter semantics that are easy to get
wrong, and the import report marks what mapped exactly, what was approximated,
and which JMeter features have no equivalent here — think-time timers,
concurrent thread groups, and non-HTTP (JDBC/FTP/LDAP/Java) samplers are
reported, never faked.

## Importing from ReadyAPI / SoapUI

Have a ReadyAPI (SoapUI) project `.xml`? Import it by following
`references/readyapi-import/README.md`. The deterministic conversion runs in the
CLI (`postman collection import --type readyapi`) — the same validated converter
the hosted ReadyAPI migration service uses, so REST/SOAP/HTTP requests, auth,
DataSource loops, environment conversion and large projects convert with no
tokens. Each Groovy script comes out as a `[MANUAL TRANSLATION REQUIRED]`
placeholder (original Groovy preserved inline); you translate those to `pm.*`
JavaScript with `references/readyapi-import/script-translation.md`, derive the
perf run from the project's LoadTests with `loadtest-to-perf.md`, and the import
report marks what needs manual work (XPath/XQuery, complex JSONPath, JDBC, WS-Security).

## Importing from Gatling

Have a Gatling project (a Java/Kotlin/Scala/JS/TS `Simulation`) instead of a
collection? Convert it by following `references/gatling-import/README.md`, then
treat the result as the collection above. There is no importer to run — you read
the source and build the collection, environment, `run.sh` and gap report, using
the files next to that README as the algorithm (`mapping.md`, `injection.md`,
`feeders.md`, `unsupported.md`). The gap report marks what mapped exactly, what
was approximated, and what has no equivalent — WebSocket/SSE and other non-HTTP
steps, arrival-rate (open-model) injection, think-time pauses, throttling and
retries are reported, never faked. Open-model injection is converted to VUs via
Little's law with the arithmetic shown, not guessed.

## Verification

Report the workload, runner, achieved traffic, latency and error metrics,
and threshold verdict. Identify generator limits or target errors that prevent
attributing the result to API capacity. See **api-testing** for functional
assertions and **ci-integration** when the measured threshold becomes a gate.

wildcard — is warned about and skipped, leaving the member working; two
members claiming one hostname fails the run. A member whose mock declares
none has no `origin` key, since `origin: []` would reach the actual service instead of the mock.

Under `--proxy` the members run on throwaway ports, so a manifest's `port` is
ignored.

## The log (`--output ndjson`)

One JSON event per line on stdout; notices go to stderr, so keep them apart.

- `listening`: every member has started; a member that fails to start
  stops the run with `Error: …` and exit code 1.
- `request`: one per request a member served.
- `summary`, on stop: `requestsServed` (under 400), `requestsFailed` (400
  and up), `uptimeMs` and `signal`. Injected failures and the simulation's
  own `400`, `404` and `502` aren't counted.
---
name: api-testing
description: Use when testing an endpoint with real HTTP requests, running collection assertions, or checking real application traffic against an API contract. Not for unit tests of internal functions. Reuses saved requests and reports what live, mocked, or captured-traffic results actually establish. Use for requests such as "test this endpoint".
---

# API Testing

Saved requests preserve the auth, payloads, variables, and assertions that make
an API check reproducible. The useful result is evidence about an intended
guarantee; a successful HTTP exchange alone does not establish correctness.

1. Choose the smallest execution mode that answers the question:

   | Evidence needed | Use |
   | --- | --- |
   | One endpoint with no saved request | `postman request <url>` |
   | Behavior of an existing saved request | `postman collection run <collection-path> -i <request-id-name-or-path>` |
   | Reusable regression checks | `postman collection run <path-or-id>` |
   | Whether a real app's calls match the contract | `postman application test` |
   | An MCP server's tools, resources, or prompts | `postman mcp` (see **mcp-testing**) |

2. Reuse a matching request under `postman/collections/` before reconstructing
   its HTTP fields. Running it through the collection retains inherited auth,
   variables, and scripts. `postman request` takes a URL, not a request YAML
   path; for an unsaved request with an existing payload file, `--body @path`
   preserves that file as the source. See **collection-schema-v3** when
   editing the saved request.
3. Derive assertions from the contract and the behavior at risk. A test that
   merely repeats the current implementation can bless its bug. Preserve
   existing guarantees and add checks for the changed behavior; put reusable
   `pm.test` assertions in the collection so later runs and teammates inherit
   them. Inline `--script-post-request` assertions suit a one-off check.
4. Choose a real or mocked target according to the claim. `--use-mock` lets a
   collection run exercise request and assertion logic without a live
   backend; `--mock` alone only starts one. `--use-mock` replaces the
   variable's whole value, base path included (see **api-mocking**). Passing
   against that mock does not verify the service the mock stands in for.
5. Reuse environment resolution with `-e` and **variables**. Use a CSV/JSON
   file through `-d` for simple iteration; use **datasets** when the inputs
   need queries, joins, or reusable views. Export a report when
   **ci-integration** needs evidence beyond terminal output; it says which
   report formats a collection supports.
6. Use `application test` when the application's actual traffic is the subject.
   It runs an existing command, such as `--command "npx playwright test"`,
   captures its traffic, and matches it against collections. `--capture-only`
   instead exports a v3 collection organized by host; that captures behavior
   without validating it. Results are recorded in the connected workspace by
   default; `--report-events=false` keeps the run local when required.

Use command-specific `-h` for supported options. Workspace resources need a
signed-in CLI; a bare URL or local collection does not require a workspace
binding.

## Verification

Report the target, tested behavior, assertion counts, and exit code. The exit
code reflects failed assertions, not HTTP status alone: a 200 can fail a test.
For application testing, distinguish matching from capture-only mode, and for
mocked runs state which real behavior remains unverified.
---
name: performance-testing
description: Use when load-testing or benchmarking an API with concurrent virtual users and latency or error thresholds, or when importing or migrating a JMeter `.jmx` plan or a Gatling simulation (Java/Kotlin/Scala/JS/TS) into a Postman collection plus a `postman performance run` configuration. Reuses a collection to probe a chosen failure mode and distinguishes target limits from load-generator limits. Use for requests such as "load test this API", "import my JMeter plan", or "convert my Gatling project to Postman".
---

# Performance Testing

A collection supplies realistic request sequences; `postman performance run`
adds concurrency and a load profile. This makes performance claims repeatable,
but only for the workload, data, and network path actually exercised.
Collections run directly: converting with `postman-to-k6` is not required.

1. Choose the failure mode before the profile: `fixed` tests sustained
   concurrency, `ramp-up` explores degradation as load grows, `spike` tests
   sudden surges, and `peak` tests staying near maximum load. Reuse the
   collection's auth and assertions, and check that its operations and data
   represent the workload rather than repeating one unusually cheap request.
2. Establish the target, VU count, duration, and effects of write requests
   before sending load. Existing user authorization for that scope is enough;
   resolve missing limits before stressing a shared or production service.
   Thresholds are evaluated after the run, so a failing gate will not stop
   traffic early. A small initial run can expose wiring failures before a
   larger authorized test.
3. Choose the runner by reachability and capacity. `local` uses this machine
   or CI runner; its CPU or network can become the bottleneck. `postman-cloud`
   moves generation to Postman's infrastructure, while
   `postman-cloud-static-ip` supports targets with IP allowlists. Verify
   reachability before interpreting connection failures as service capacity.
4. Set thresholds that represent the user's objective, such as
   `--pass-if "less_than(p95, 500)"`. Supported metrics include `avg`, `p90`,
   `p95`, `p99`, `error_rate`, and `rps`; latency alone can look good when
   requests fail quickly. Use `postman performance run -h` for current syntax,
   units, and runner-specific options.
5. Isolate test data where concurrent writes would collide. **datasets**
   supports controlled row distribution across VUs; setup/teardown collections
   on hosted runners execute once around the test, not once per iteration.
   `--use-mock` can baseline collection/script overhead, but its numbers
   cannot establish the real backend's capacity.

## Importing from JMeter

Have a JMeter `.jmx` instead of a collection? Import it by following
`references/jmeter-import/README.md`, then treat the result as the collection
above. Its mapping table carries the JMeter semantics that are easy to get
wrong, and the import report marks what mapped exactly, what was approximated,
and which JMeter features have no equivalent here — think-time timers,
concurrent thread groups, and non-HTTP (JDBC/FTP/LDAP/Java) samplers are
reported, never faked.

## Importing from ReadyAPI / SoapUI

Have a ReadyAPI (SoapUI) project `.xml`? Import it by following
`references/readyapi-import/README.md`. The deterministic conversion runs in the
CLI (`postman collection import --type readyapi`) — the same validated converter
the hosted ReadyAPI migration service uses, so REST/SOAP/HTTP requests, auth,
DataSource loops, environment conversion and large projects convert with no
tokens. Each Groovy script comes out as a `[MANUAL TRANSLATION REQUIRED]`
placeholder (original Groovy preserved inline); you translate those to `pm.*`
JavaScript with `references/readyapi-import/script-translation.md`, derive the
perf run from the project's LoadTests with `loadtest-to-perf.md`, and the import
report marks what needs manual work (XPath/XQuery, complex JSONPath, JDBC, WS-Security).

## Importing from Gatling

Have a Gatling project (a Java/Kotlin/Scala/JS/TS `Simulation`) instead of a
collection? Convert it by following `references/gatling-import/README.md`, then
treat the result as the collection above. There is no importer to run — you read
the source and build the collection, environment, `run.sh` and gap report, using
the files next to that README as the algorithm (`mapping.md`, `injection.md`,

was approximated, and what has no equivalent — WebSocket/SSE and other non-HTTP
steps, arrival-rate (open-model) injection, think-time pauses, throttling and
retries are reported, never faked. Open-model injection is converted to VUs via
Little's law with the arithmetic shown, not guessed.

## Verification

Report the workload, runner, achieved traffic, latency and error metrics,
and threshold verdict. Identify generator limits or target errors that prevent
attributing the result to API capacity. See **api-testing** for functional
assertions and **ci-integration** when the measured threshold becomes a gate.

---
name: api-mocking
description: Use when something needs an API that isn't built or reachable yet (a frontend, client or demo), when other teams should build against your API before it ships, or when asked to mock an API or fake a backend. Finds, builds, runs and publishes a stand-in for one API — a published mock when its owner or a verified publisher has one, otherwise one built from its spec or collection that behaves like the real API, stateful when callers write then read. To run and test your own code against the services it calls, use api-simulation. Covers `postman mock` and `postman dependency add mock`.
---

# API Mocking

A mock is a folder, `config.yaml` plus a handler such as `default.js`, that
answers like an API. The handler is a Node HTTP server that calls
`listen(process.env.PORT)`. It loads as CommonJS even in an ESM project, so
`import` fails: use `require`. The same mock lives in your repo
(`postman/mocks/<name>/`, run with `postman mock run`, no sign-in needed),
in a Postman workspace after `postman mock push`, where other teams pull it
from, and on a mock server after `postman mock deploy`, for callers that
can't run it themselves.

Several APIs at once, for a service, a frontend or a test suite? Use
`api-simulation`, which gets each member's mock here.

## Use a published mock first

When the API belongs to another team or a third-party provider, look for a
published mock before writing one: a maintained mock encodes the contract
and the service's state; yours encodes a guess.

Every step below needs a signed-in CLI. Check `postman status` first; signed
out, skip to building one and say the search was skipped.

1. Find the mock.
   - **Another team's service:** find the owner's workspace with
     `postman search workspaces "<service>" -o json`. Name the service
     plainly, as your code does, not by what it returns: a description
     matches lookalike services. Prefer a Git-connected workspace
     (`isGitConnected`) named for that service, then list its mocks with
     `postman mock list -w <workspaceId> --json`. `postman search mocks`
     misses some, and a same-named mock in another workspace isn't the
     owner's.
   - **A third-party API,** such as a payment or email provider: search
     mocks directly with
     `postman search mocks "<provider>" --ownership all -o json`. The
     workspace that holds one is rarely named for the provider, and the
     default ownership searches only your organization. Prefer a `codeMock`
     named for the provider from a verified organization
     (`organization.isVerified`).

   A `classicMock` only replays a collection's saved examples: `postman mock`
   can't pull or run it, so call one at `https://<mockId>.mock.pstmn.io` with
   `postman request`, or generate a code mock from its collection.
2. Pull it with `postman dependency add mock <mockId>`, run the folder it
   writes with `postman mock run`, and use it as it is. Commit
   `postman/.dependencies/` when CI should run it without signing in;
   otherwise CI restores it with `dependency install`, which needs a sign-in
   (see **api-discovery**). Never edit `postman/.dependencies/`:
   `dependency update` overwrites it, so copy a mock to `postman/mocks/` to
   change it. A mock is code that runs as you; pull only from publishers you
   trust.

## Or build one that behaves like the real API

Callers shouldn't be able to tell the difference on the paths they use. A
mock that returns invented JSON passes your tests and fails against the
real service.

- **Start from the contract.** `postman mock generate <spec or collection>`
  writes each documented response. It's a replay: a `POST` and a later
  `GET` share nothing, and it accepts any request, so a call that breaks the
  contract still gets its answer. `x-mock-response-code` picks only a
  documented status; any other code gets the default 200, so put the errors
  callers handle (the unknown-id 404, the conflict 409, the bad-input 400) in
  the contract. From a spec
  it serves the server URL's base path (`/v2/...`); from a collection,
  routes start after the base-URL variable. `--update` regenerates the
  handler and overwrites your edits. With no contract, write it from how
  your code calls the API and say what you assumed.
- **Set `interceptRequests: true` in `config.yaml`.** Without it `req.body`
  and `req.query` are undefined, `x-mock-session` is ignored, and a throw in
  an async handler kills the mock instead of returning a `500`.
- **Make it stateful when callers write then read.** Keep records in
  `pm.state`, seed them on first use, add a reset route so a test can start
  clean, and answer an unknown id with the real 404. Every `mock run` starts
  empty.
- **Know who shares state.** Locally, all callers share one state unless
  each sends `x-mock-session: <id>`. A mock server deployed from the CLI
  isolates each caller: one that keeps neither the same `x-mock-session` nor
  the `pm_mock_session` cookie starts from the seed on every request, so its
  `POST` and later `GET` never meet.
- **Scenarios** are named handlers in `config.yaml`'s `scenarios` list, picked
  per request with `x-mock-scenario: <name>`. An unknown name falls back to
  the default locally but is a `404` on a mock server.

## Check it against the contract

`postman mock run` prints the URL it bound; a busy configured port moves
unless you pass `--port`, so take the URL from that line. Nothing reloads:
restart it after an edit.

A mock checked against the handler you just wrote proves nothing, so call
it with requests from the contract: `postman request`, or the API's
collection with
`postman collection run <collection> --use-mock "{{baseUrl}} mock:postman/mocks/<name>"`
(`--mock` alone only starts it). That form replaces the variable's whole
value, base path included, so a mock generated from a spec that serves
`/v2/...` answers `404`; start that one with `--mock <path> --port <n>` and
pass `--env-var "baseUrl=http://localhost:<n>/v2"`. To check your own calls
against a contract, compare each one, from the code or a simulation log,
with the spec; the mock won't reject a wrong one.

## Publish it for other teams

- **Push it to the service's own workspace,** the one this repo is linked
  to or the one the user names, never one chosen by name match: other
  teams' simulations look there. Signed out, the push fails but the local
  mock still works; build it, say so and ask the user to sign in. Keep it
  honest: change the mock in the same PR as the API and run the API's
  collection against it.
- **Deploy only when a caller needs a URL.** The server takes a slug of 3–32
  lowercase letters, digits and single hyphens, starting and ending with a
  letter or digit; the CLI accepts more, and its default can be too long.
  It's private: callers send an API key as `x-api-key`, or, if they can
  view the workspace, an access token as `x-access-token`. Deploying needs a paid plan; a team's first
  server can take minutes to answer, and teams that review deploys hold them
  for approval. Each later `push` changes what every caller of the server
  gets, so treat it as a release, not a backup.
- **Write it for where it runs.** A mock server runs each scenario as one
  file with Node's built-ins, not `fs` or `child_process`: no local
  `require`s, no `pm.mock` examples, no environment, no console output, and
  no caller `authorization`, `cookie` or `x-api-key` headers. A mock that
  relies on any of these works locally and breaks once deployed.
- **Ask before `--public`.** It serves the mock and its data to anyone with
  the URL, and a scripted redeploy can't make it private again.

## Before you say it's done

A mock isn't done because it started. Call it: a documented error comes
back, a valid scenario changes the response, a `POST` then `GET` shows state
if it should. Say where it runs and who can call it, where it lives, and
what you assumed.
